rows.label: Share of money moved by a meta charity that donors wouldn't otherwise have given (new money)

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Effective Giving Incubation report
source.quote: the percentage of money raised that is counterfactual (i.e. would not have otherwise been donated) is about 50% of the total raised
source.note: Low: Ambitious Impact's own 35% for a charity evaluator (Better Futures Guide sheet, Main CEA!B34). High: our judgment for an organisation that mostly recruits new givers.

rows.explainer: Of the money a meta charity moves (an evaluator, a fundraiser, an effective-giving organisation), the share that would not have been given at all without it. The rest is shifted money: given anyway, now to a better charity. Every meta model on the site uses this one figure in our view (docs/normalization.md 2.8), in place of each evaluator's own: Ambitious Impact's 35% for evaluators, our earlier 40% for The Life You Can Save. 50%, from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Chance that a new, not-yet-proven meta organisation succeeds

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Establishing a livelihoods non-profit evaluator (2025): CEA, 'Probability of success'
source.note: Average of Ambitious Impact's three methods (comparable evaluators 63.5%, its incubated charities 50%, its statements on effective-giving organisations 53.75%); the range is the lowest and highest method.

rows.explainer: One chance of success for every meta organisation that has not yet shown results (an idea report's new charity). Ambitious Impact's own average of three methods, 55.7%; the range runs from its lowest method (50%) to its highest (63.5%). Established organisations with a track record (The Life You Can Save) take no such step.

rows.label: Share of effective donations going to improving human wellbeing

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2020–2022 impact evaluation
source.quote: Nearly 60% of our donors' recorded donations go to the cause area of improving human wellbeing
source.note: Range: Giving What We Can's split for non-pledge (43%) and pledge (65%) donations, posted by its staff with the evaluation.

rows.explainer: Where money moved to effective charities goes when the donor chooses the cause: Giving What We Can's recorded donations, 2020–2022. Used for meta charities whose donors give across causes (CEARCH); an organisation that only moves money within one cause (The Life You Can Save, Better Futures Guide) uses that cause's value alone.

rows.label: Share of effective donations going to animal welfare

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2020–2022 impact evaluation
source.quote: slightly below 10% of recorded donations go improving animal welfare
source.note: Range: pledge (7%) and non-pledge (13%) donations.

rows.explainer: Giving What We Can's recorded donations, 2020–2022: about one dollar in ten goes to animal welfare.

rows.label: Share of effective donations going to creating a better future (longtermist causes)

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2020–2022 impact evaluation
source.quote: slightly above 10% to creating a better future
source.note: Range: pledge (11%) and non-pledge (15%) donations. The remaining ~20% went to unknown or several causes.

rows.explainer: Giving What We Can's recorded donations, 2020–2022: about one dollar in ten goes to reducing catastrophic risks and other longtermist causes. The rest, about 20%, went to unknown or several cause areas; the site values that part at the average of the known destinations, so it drops out of the mix.

rows.label: Value of a dollar given to longtermist charities, in units of value (not valued: 0)
rows.explainer: Said openly: the site has no model that puts reducing catastrophic risk on its scale of healthy years, so a dollar moved to longtermist charities counts as 0 here. That understates meta charities whose donors give to these causes, and is a choice, not a finding. Change it on a page to see what it does.

rows.label: GiveWell's 2024 funding to its Top Charities: Against Malaria Foundation's share

source.title: GiveWell, GiveWell's 2024 metrics and impact
source.quote: $150 million (50% of the total directed to Top Charities) going to the Against Malaria Foundation for insecticide-treated nets
source.note: $150m of the $303m GiveWell directed to its four Top Charities in 2024 ($150m AMF, $87m Malaria Consortium SMC, $54m Helen Keller Intl VAS, $12m New Incentives).

rows.explainer: The value of a dollar moved to global health and poverty charities is GiveWell's four Top Charities, each at its live result on this site, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024.

rows.label: GiveWell's 2024 funding to its Top Charities: Malaria Consortium's (SMC) share

source.title: GiveWell, GiveWell's 2024 metrics and impact
source.quote: $87 million (28%) to Malaria Consortium for its seasonal malaria chemoprevention program

rows.explainer: Malaria Consortium's seasonal malaria chemoprevention: its share of GiveWell's 2024 Top Charity funding.

rows.label: GiveWell's 2024 funding to its Top Charities: Helen Keller Intl's (vitamin A) share

source.title: GiveWell, GiveWell's 2024 metrics and impact
source.quote: $54 million (18%) to Helen Keller Intl for its vitamin A supplementation program

rows.explainer: Helen Keller Intl's vitamin A supplementation: its share of GiveWell's 2024 Top Charity funding.

rows.label: GiveWell's 2024 funding to its Top Charities: New Incentives' share

source.title: GiveWell, GiveWell's 2024 metrics and impact
source.quote: around $12 million (4%) to New Incentives for its program of conditional cash transfers to increase vaccinations

rows.explainer: New Incentives' conditional cash transfers for vaccination: its share of GiveWell's 2024 Top Charity funding.

rows.label: Value of where shifted money would otherwise have gone, as a multiple of GiveDirectly's live result

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Establishing a livelihoods non-profit evaluator (2025): CEA, 'From "shifted money"'
source.note: Ambitious Impact values shifted money by the gain over GiveDirectly. Low: money shifted from ordinary charities that do little measurable good. High: from charities at GiveWell's funding bar, about 3× GiveDirectly's November 2024 estimate.

rows.explainer: Shifted money (given anyway, now to a better charity) is credited only with the gain: the value where it goes, less the value where it would have gone. The site takes the second as GiveDirectly's live result, as Ambitious Impact does: donors who give to a meta charity's recommendations would otherwise mostly have given to good but less proven charities. 1×, from 0 (ordinary charities) to 3× (charities as good as GiveWell's bar).

rows.label: A marginal dollar's result as a share of the organisation's past average result

source.title: CEARCH, Giving What We Can's marginal giving multiplier (2025); Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 impact evaluation
source.note: The only published comparisons of a marginal against an average result for an established organisation: CEARCH puts Giving What We Can's marginal 2025 multiplier at about 13x against its 2020–22 average of 30x (0.43), and its 2023–24 marginal at 17.6% of the average; Giving What We Can expects its marginal multiplier to be much closer to its average (up to 1). 50%, from 18% to 100%: our judgment.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, one figure for every model whose result is an established organisation's past average (money moved over total cost, or tonnes from past campaigns over past budgets): the next dollar does less than the average dollar did, because an organisation spends first on what works best. GiveWell's, Ambitious Impact's and other forward-looking estimates are already marginal and don't take it. Used by The Life You Can Save (its 3-year leverage ratio) and the climate models built on past budgets and past wins (Clean Air Task Force, Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Carbon180, Evergreen 2021, Future Cleantech Architects, Good Food Institute, Industrious Labs, Opportunity Green, Terrapraxis).

rows.label: Money a new meta organisation moves if it fails, as a share of what it would move if it succeeded

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Establishing a livelihoods non-profit evaluator (2025): CEA, 'If charity is unsuccessful, what % of successful money moved will be moved'

rows.explainer: The failure branch of the shared success step (docs/normalization.md 2.8): a meta organisation that doesn't succeed still moves some money while it runs. Ambitious Impact's 20%, its own judgment. CEARCH and Better Futures Guide both use it.

rows.label: Years a new meta organisation runs (and spends) before closing if it fails

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Establishing a livelihoods non-profit evaluator (2025): CEA, operating costs if unsuccessful (years 1–3, none in years 4–5)

rows.explainer: The failure branch of the shared success step: a failing meta organisation spends for its first three years and then stops (Ambitious Impact's Better Futures Guide sheet). CEARCH's model, which charged all five years of costs to a failure, now uses the same three.
